analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act rule requiring large employers to offer health coverage or pay fines.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 32 Republican senators, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2013 and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase the part of the Affordable Care Act that fines large employers—those with more than 50 full-time workers—if they don't offer their employees health insurance, and it would erase the requirement that those employers report to the Treasury what coverage they provide. In practice, large companies could stop offering coverage without penalty. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers with more than 50 full-time employees gain the most: they would no longer face fines for failing to offer affordable coverage and would no longer have to file coverage reports with the IRS. Some employees might keep wages that employers would otherwise spend on health benefits, but that tradeoff is not guaranteed in the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act's employer mandate, so companies with more than 50 full-time employees would pay no fine for failing to offer minimum essential coverage [S2][S3].
Also repeals the requirement that large employers report to the Treasury Secretary on the coverage they provide, ending the paperwork and compliance burden those filings create [S2][S3].
Applies the tax code as if the mandate and reporting rules had never been enacted, so no related penalties, assessments, or recordkeeping would survive [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers at large firms that choose to drop coverage would bear the main cost, since the mandate was designed to make employer coverage available and affordable; anyone losing employer coverage would have to rely on the individual marketplaces or go uninsured. The repeal would also reduce federal revenue, since the employer fines were a source of funds for the health law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employees who could lose employer coverage

drawbacks.text: Without the fine, some large employers would have an incentive to stop offering coverage and let employees buy insurance on their own, shifting workers onto the marketplaces or leaving them uninsured [S2].
The employer fine was one of the Affordable Care Act's revenue sources; repealing it would add to federal deficits, meaning other taxpayers or programs would eventually absorb the difference [S2].
The bill contains no replacement mechanism to keep employer coverage affordable or available, so workers' access to job-based insurance would depend entirely on each employer's voluntary choice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, certain benefit to large employers by removing a fine and a reporting requirement, but the benefits to workers are speculative—lower wages are possible but not guaranteed—while the risks are concrete: dropped coverage for employees and lost federal revenue. As written, the gains and losses fall on very different groups.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on February 28, 2013, joined by 27 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
A total of 31 Republican senators cosponsored the bill [S4].
No further action was recorded—the Finance Committee never marked up the bill and the Senate never voted on it—so it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Affordable Care Act's employer mandate and reporting rules remained in place, and large employers continued to face the fines and paperwork the bill would have removed. Workers' access to employer-sponsored coverage was not put at risk of repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employer health mandate stayed; large employers kept the obligation

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA employer mandate and reporting requirement [S1][S3].

for.name: 31 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it full-throated Republican support but no Democratic cosponsor [S4].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took the bill up; it saw no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 32 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would remove the fines and coverage-reporting duties the Affordable Care Act imposes on them, freeing them from a direct cost. The tradeoff is that their employees' access to job-based coverage would depend on voluntary employer choices rather than a legal requirement [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Employers and payroll/HR compliance service providers
industries.note: Companies selling compliance software and benefits-administration services to large firms would lose demand if the coverage-reporting requirement disappeared. This is a minor, secondary effect of the repeal [S2].
